newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bullish Allianz looks to industry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bullish Allianz looks to industry.

text.p: Giant German insurer Allianz AG Holding on Wednesday said its profits should rise at least 10 percent this year with underwriting earnings to break even for the first time in seven years, if claims stay modest.

Business had gone well in the first quarter, it said, with earnings higher and premiums up more than 12 percent on the year-ago period, albeit chiefly due to the consolidation of the large health insurer Vereinte Kranken and currency effects, without which sales would have risen only 1.3 percent.

The company, just ousted from the position of Europe's biggest insurer after the merger of UAP and Axa of France, also declared its aim of becoming the world's top industrial insurer, and said it would offer alternative risk transfer (ART) products from a new Zurich-based unit as of autumn.

"We want to break even in the Allianz Group's underwriting result in 1997 as well as achieve moderate double digit profit growth and make further progress in the growth markets of Central and Eastern Europe and Asia," chairman Henning Schulte-Noelle told a news conference.

Allianz had already reported key figures for 1996, when its net profit rose 10.7 percent to 2.24 billion marks ($1.3 billion) as it narrowed its underwriting loss, in the red since 1990, to 148 million marks from 684 million marks.
Its outlook, which analysts said matched positive expectations, was well received earlier in the markets and shares rose 1.2 percent to a new record high of 383.50 marks.
But the shares were later dragged lower by a falling market and in late electronic trade were down over two percent at 371 marks.
Elaborating on its industrial insurance plans, Allianz said it would set up the specialist ART unit for industry clients in Zurich with capital of 500 Swiss francs ($352).

ART allows clients to combine coverage of insurance risks with market and financial risks, an area that is becoming increasingly significant in Europe and the United States, according to Schulte-Noelle.

Board member Reiner Hagemann said he was confident Allianz could raise its industrial business sales by 50 percent from the current two billion marks by the year 2000. The company is to co-ordinate this business under an international committee.

Allianz is predicting an 11 percent rise in group sales this year to 83 billion marks, of which just two billion marks will be due to internal growth, the rest being the effect of consolidating Vereinte and the first full-year consolidation of the Hermes credit insurance group and the Swiss Berner unit.
Another key part of Allianz's strategy would be developing more direct distribution channels and increasing sales cooperation-operations with banks world-wide, Schulte-Noelle said.

However Schulte-Noelle, echoing other leaders in the German financial services sector, downplayed talk of imminent upheavals in the German banking landscape and speculation that Allianz might be on the look-out to buy into a top German bank.
"Of course we are interested in this process but we are not in a position in which we are taking an active role in pushing the situation forward," he said.
Schulte-Noelle said he did not expect a big financial merger in the next two years but conceded: "The boundaries between banking and insurance are getting more blurred."

The Allianz chief also addressed the thorny question of the class action U.S. lawsuit pending against it and six other insurers charging it with concealing assets from victims of Nazi persecution -- charges the company is anxious to clarify.

Extensive research had failed to yield a single valid claim, Schulte-Noelle said. Allianz launched a hotline service to help relatives of Nazi victims get information, so far attracting 680 inquiries but no concrete result.
"It would be personally unbearable to me if there were some sum on our books that did not belong to us, but rather to Nazi victims. As far as we know, this is not the case," he said.
"We want to be really sure about this. Therefore we will continue with our search, lawsuit or no lawsuit."

Allianz is sifting though the files remaining from the Nazi era but has been hampered by the fact that these are arranged by policy number, not name. The bulk of claims, it says, have already been settled by the German government. ($ = 1.702 German Marks) ($ = 1.421 Swiss Francs)
